topStories.headline: Tetra Tech Pays $97 Million to Close Federal Hunters Point Case — But Neighborhood Residents See Almost Nothing
topStories.dek: A federal judge approved the long-contested settlement this month, closing the government's case against the contractor that falsified radioactive soil samples — even as more than 300 neighborhood homeowners were separately denied any compensation.
topStories.body:
More than a decade after a contractor hired to clean up the former Hunters Point Naval Shipyard was caught faking radiological testing results, the federal government's case formally closed this week. Tetra Tech EC Inc. will pay a total of $97 million — $57 million to resolve False Claims Act allegations brought by the U.S. Department of Justice, and another $40 million tied to ongoing Superfund cleanup costs — to settle claims that its workers substituted clean soil for contaminated samples and falsified data between 2003 and 2014.

U.S. District Judge James Donato had initially rejected the settlement, saying prosecutors had not adequately explained why the payout was proportionate to the scale of the fraud. After further briefings, Donato on August 13 deemed the agreement 'fair, adequate, and reasonable.' Tetra Tech is not admitting wrongdoing. Whistleblowers — former Tetra Tech employees and contractors who first exposed the scheme — will share approximately $11.97 million of the total recovery.

Almost none of the $97 million flows directly to Bayview–Hunters Point residents. More than 300 homeowners on Parcel A — the only completed residential section of the shipyard development — had argued separately that the fraud tanked their property values. On August 4, Judge Donato dismissed that lawsuit, ruling that the federal Price-Anderson Act, a 1957 law designed to shield the nuclear industry from certain liability, bars claims based purely on financial loss. A separate group of roughly 6,000 Bayview residents who sued Tetra Tech received a February settlement worth $1.5 million in total — roughly $230 per plaintiff.

Environmental justice advocates say the legal closure does not mean the contamination threat is resolved. The Navy continues testing and remediation at the 443-acre Superfund site, and as of recent Navy progress reports, crews are still verifying earlier radiological work, addressing mercury in groundwater, and investigating radioactive objects found in areas not previously flagged for cleanup. Greenaction for Health and Environmental Justice has called for independent verification of the site before any further development proceeds.

topStories.headline: Visitacion Valley Launches Its First-Ever Night Market Tonight on Leland Avenue
topStories.dek: The inaugural Visitacion Valley Night Market fills Leland Avenue with food vendors, live music, and dancing this evening — the first in a two-month series backed by the Civic Joy Fund.
topStories.body:
Visitacion Valley hosts its first-ever night market tonight, Friday August 28, along Leland Avenue between Bayshore Boulevard and Peabody Street, from 4 to 8:30 p.m. The free, all-ages event features food vendors, local shopping, live music, street dancing, family activities, and community organization booths, organized with support from the Civic Joy Fund and the Southside Community Development Corporation.

The market is the first of two planned for 2026. The series continues on Friday, September 25, also from 4 to 8:30 p.m. on the same stretch of Leland Avenue. Organizers are billing the event as a celebration of the neighborhood's culture, diversity, and community spirit.

Muni riders should note service disruptions. The SFMTA has imposed a street closure on Leland Avenue between Peabody Street and Bayshore Boulevard from noon to 10 p.m. today, and the 56 Rutland bus line will reroute around the market area for the duration of the event.

Leland Avenue is the commercial spine of Visitacion Valley, lined with small businesses and eateries. Organizers are hoping the market format — loose, walkable, and free — gives those businesses a chance to connect with neighbors and draw visitors who might not otherwise make it to this corner of the city.

topStories.headline: SCRAP Reopens in Bayview With a Permanent Home Five Times Its Former Size
topStories.dek: The beloved 50-year-old creative reuse nonprofit opened its doors at 141 Industrial Street this month, landing in a building it now owns outright after losing its longtime school-district warehouse lease.
topStories.body:
SCRAP — the Scroungers' Center for Reusable Art Parts — celebrated its grand reopening on August 15 at 141 Industrial Street in the Bayview, completing a move that for years felt uncertain. The nonprofit, which collects donated materials that might otherwise be discarded and sells them at low cost to artists, teachers, and makers, had operated out of a San Francisco Unified School District warehouse at 2150 Newcomb Avenue for 25 years. SFUSD is converting that site into a central kitchen funded by a $790 million bond passed by voters in November 2024.

The new space is roughly five times the footprint of the old warehouse, and — for the first time in SCRAP's 50-year history — the organization owns the building outright. The nonprofit purchased the building from the Calvary Hill Community Church after the church went into foreclosure; the church continues to rent the second floor as SCRAP's tenant, while SCRAP occupies the ground floor, which adds nearly 19,000 square feet for bookbinding and basket-making workshops and its ever-changing inventory.

SCRAP was co-founded by artist Ruth Asawa and Anne Marie Theilen. It also hosts creative workshops, partners with local schools, and provides art materials to teachers for little or no cost. Staff say the expanded space will allow the center to accept an estimated 100 additional tons of donated materials each year and grow its after-school and corporate programming. The nonprofit recently launched a $7.5 million capital campaign to support the move and upgrades. The August 15 grand reopening featured a ribbon-cutting, tree planting, free hands-on workshop activities, and ice cream.

moreNews.headline: Bayview Oyster Bar on Track to Open on Third Street in September
moreNews.body: Bayview Oyster Bar, the modern seafood restaurant from chef and Bayview native April Spears, is on track to open at 5114 Third Street in September. The spot will feature a raw bar at the front, a seafood counter, roughly 25 dining seats, and — eventually — a backyard patio decorated with historic black-and-white photographs of the neighborhood. The menu will focus on Dungeness crab, king salmon, and oysters, with some dishes prepared over open flame in a style inspired by Spears' Louisiana roots. The restaurant is one of nine businesses receiving support through the city's Storefront Opportunity Grant program, which has been credited with spurring a broader restaurant revival along the Third Street corridor. Spears previously ran Auntie April's and Cafe Envy in the Bayview before both closed during the pandemic.

moreNews.headline: Gumbo Social Reopens After Six-Week Retooling
moreNews.body: Gumbo Social, the popular soul food restaurant at 5176 Third Street in the Bayview, reopened August 17 after a planned six-week closure for equipment upgrades and operational improvements. Owner Dontaye Ball described the closure as a deliberate investment in the restaurant's long-term sustainability, writing that the alternative was risking closure within six months. Ball is also working toward adding a walk-up takeout window that would extend service hours into the evening, with a goal of launching the window by September. The restaurant, now in its third year as a brick-and-mortar, has become one of the most visible Black-owned businesses on the Third Street corridor.

moreNews.headline: Crocker Amazon Park Renovation Moves Through Design Phase as Community Debate Continues
moreNews.body: The proposed $50 million renovation of Crocker Amazon Park's baseball and softball fields — backed by a $28 million grant from the San Francisco Giants and a $5 million gift from Willie Mays' Say Hey Foundation — continued through its design and environmental review phase this month, with the Recreation and Park Department posting an update on August 13. The Rec and Park Commission approved renaming the complex the Willie Mays Fields of Champions in April and recommended the Board of Supervisors accept the Giants' grant, but community opposition from the group Keep Crocker Real remains active. Opponents object to plans to remove more than 100 mature trees and replace natural grass with artificial turf across the park's western half. The project still requires Board of Supervisors approval and environmental review; construction is targeted to begin no earlier than 2027.

moreNews.headline: Hunters Point Homeowners Denied Damages as Federal Shipyard Settlement Closes
moreNews.body: As the federal government's fraud case against Tetra Tech EC closed this month with a $97 million settlement, more than 300 homeowners on Parcel A of the Hunters Point Shipyard development received no share of those funds. On August 4, U.S. District Judge James Donato ruled that the federal Price-Anderson Act — a 1957 nuclear liability law — shields Tetra Tech from homeowner claims for economic damages such as diminished property values. A separate group of roughly 6,000 Bayview residents who sued Tetra Tech received a February 2026 settlement totaling $1.5 million — approximately $230 per plaintiff. Environmental advocates, including Greenaction for Health and Environmental Justice, say the cleanup of the 443-acre Superfund site remains incomplete and are pressing Mayor Daniel Lurie and other officials to support independent testing and greater community oversight as the Navy continues work at the site.
